---
title: "Quiz: Chan–Vese"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Energy $E = \sum_{\text{in}}(I - c_1)^2 + \sum_{\text{out}}(I - c_2)^2 + \lambda\cdot\text{Length} + \nu\cdot\text{Area}_{\text{in}}$; $\phi < 0$ inside.

---

**Q1.** For a fixed curve, why are the best $c_1$ and $c_2$ the mean grey levels inside and outside?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which number $c$ minimises $\sum (I_p - c)^2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The derivative of $\sum_p (I_p - c)^2$ with respect to $c$ is $-2\sum_p(I_p - c)$, zero when $c$ is the mean. Each sum involves only its own $c$, so both are means.
:::

---

**Q2.** $c_1 = 0.7$ (inside) and $c_2 = 0.3$. A pixel near the curve has grey level 0.45. Does it join the inside or the outside (with $\lambda = \nu = 0$)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $(I - c_1)^2$ and $(I - c_2)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(0.45 - 0.7)^2 = 0.0625$, $(0.45 - 0.3)^2 = 0.0225$: it is closer to $c_2$ and goes outside. With $\lambda = 0$ the rule is a threshold at $(c_1 + c_2)/2 = 0.5$.
:::

---

**Q3.** What does Chan–Vese with $\lambda = 0$ compute, and which method from the thresholding day is it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Alternate the two steps without a length term.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each pixel joins the closer mean, i.e. a threshold at $(c_1 + c_2)/2$; then the means are recomputed. At convergence the threshold is the midpoint of the two class means: the isodata (two-means) fixed point.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does a large $\lambda$ remove a thin bar but keep a large disk of the same grey level?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the data gain (area) with the boundary cost (length).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keeping an object saves data cost in proportion to its **area** and costs $\lambda$ times its **perimeter**. A thin bar has a long perimeter for its area; a disk of radius $r$ has area $\pi r^2$ for perimeter $2\pi r$, so its gain per unit boundary grows with $r$. The bar goes first: the shrinking bias of the graph cuts day.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why does Chan–Vese not need to smooth the image, while geodesic active contours do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to noise in a mean over many pixels?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It uses no derivatives of the image, only sums over regions: noise averages out in $c_1$ and $c_2$, and the length term removes isolated misassigned pixels. Gradients, in contrast, amplify noise.
:::

---

**Q6.** The background of an image gets brighter from left to right, and at the right side it is as bright as the objects. What goes wrong with Chan–Vese?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many grey levels does the model allow for the background?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The model has one constant per region. The bright part of the background is closer to the object mean than to the (darker) background mean, so it is labelled object. Edge-based methods, which only look at local differences, cope better with such shading.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is a grid of small blobs a better start than one small circle in the background?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What are $c_1$ and $c_2$ at the start, and how strongly do the data then push?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A small circle in the background has $c_1 \approx c_2 \approx$ the background grey level: the data term barely distinguishes the regions and the length term shrinks the circle away (a local minimum). A grid samples every region from the start; pixels flip towards the closer mean everywhere, $c_1$ and $c_2$ separate quickly, and the result does not depend on where the objects are.
:::

---

**Q8.** What does the width $\varepsilon$ of $\delta_\varepsilon$ change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pixels does the update reach?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The update of each pixel is weighted by $\delta_\varepsilon(\phi)$. Narrow: only pixels near the curve change, the curve moves like a front. Wide: pixels far from the curve change too, so new objects and holes can appear away from the start curve.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Write the Chan–Vese energy with the Heaviside function $H(\phi)$ and derive $\phi_t$ by gradient descent (constant $c_1$, $c_2$).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\tfrac{d}{d\phi}H(\phi) = \delta(\phi)$; the length is $\int\delta(\phi)|\nabla\phi|$, whose variation is $-\delta(\phi)\kappa$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$E = \int(I - c_1)^2(1 - H) + \int(I - c_2)^2H + \lambda\int\delta(\phi)|\nabla\phi| + \nu\int(1 - H)$ ($H = 1$ outside). Then $\delta E/\delta\phi = \delta(\phi)[-(I - c_1)^2 + (I - c_2)^2 - \lambda\kappa - \nu]$, and $\phi_t = -\delta E/\delta\phi = \delta(\phi)[\lambda\kappa + \nu + (I - c_1)^2 - (I - c_2)^2]$.
:::
